title: InMotion Hosting Review 2026: Hosting for Tech-Savvy Users, Not for Everyone Else - CNET
headings: Value: A solid choice for monetized websites, not for personal sites
Ease of use: Underwhelming, especially for first-time website owners
The purchase process includes sneaky upsells
Website and server management tools aren’t great, especially for beginners
Security: Solid protection from various threats, but little recourse if something goes wrong
Customer service: Some of it is great, some of it isn’t
Knowledge base and tutorials lack visual materials
Reputation is mostly good, with some concerns
InMotion can work for tech-savvy users, but it’s not the best choice
text: Sarah Tew/CNET InMotion Hosting Review 6.8 See at InMotion Hosting Pros & Cons Fast support via live chat and email Easy cPanel access ideal for technical users like developers and web admins Ugly, often overwhelming user interface Poor server performance Minimal WordPress tools InMotion Hosting offers various web hosting packages that, on paper, work for everything from personal blogs to enterprise business sites. However, its poorly designed user interface and unreliable servers make it difficult to recommend for most people. I only recommend using InMotion if you’re technically oriented, like a developer (or working with one), and even then, you can get better value and performance from a company like Ionos. I built a site with InMotion’s WordPress hosting and tracked uptime and server speed for one week to determine its effectiveness. Unfortunately, the clunky interface and poor server performance left me frustrated on several occasions. Furthermore, InMotion’s customer service was inconsistent, providing a pleasant experience via live chat and email but making me wait an unreasonable amount of time for phone support. Overall, InMotion Hosting works best for tech-savvy users. But you’ll find a better experience, with faster servers, more reliable uptime and polished user interfaces with other top web hosts. More from CNET Value: A solid choice for monetized websites, not for personal sites Key takeaway: InMotion’s generous storage and bandwidth are great for business websites, but its unusually high introductory rates and mid-range renewal costs may be off-putting if you’re building a personal website. Hosting type Starting price Best for Shared Hosting $17 a month, $57 for the first year (renews at $180 annually), $120 for the first two years (renews at $336 biannually) or $180 for the first three years (renews at $504 triannually) Simple websites like blogs, for-fun hobby sites and small business websites not using WordPress WordPress Hosting $16 a month, $63 for the first year (renews at $186 annually), $132 for the first two years (renews at $348 biannually) or $198 for the first three years (renews at $522 triannually) Simple websites like blogs, for-fun hobby sites and small business websites using WordPress VPS Hosting $17 for the first month (renews at $37 monthly), $180 for the first year (renews at $324 annually), $336 for the first two years (renews at $648 biannually) or $360 for the first three years (renews at $612 triannually) Websites requiring significant storage, bandwidth, or server customization InMotion Hosting prices are higher than average — closer to SiteGround than to Hostinger — but the expense is offset by ample storage and bandwidth (which dictates the number of visitors your site can handle). As such, InMotion Hosting provides solid value for business websites, especially ones with lots of large files. However, you’ll probably want to go with another host if you’re building a personal site or a hobby site with no plans to monetize. Shared and WordPress hosting Shared and WordPress hosting are ideal for simple websites like blogs, for-fun hobby sites or small business websites thanks to their affordability and easy setup. InMotion’s introductory rates are higher than typical, while renewal costs sit firmly in the middle between budget-friendly companies like Hostinger and pricier hosts like SiteGround. Notably, InMotion Hosting’s lowest-tier Launch plans include more storage than most web hosts, including the more expensive SiteGround. Of the hosts I’ve tested so far, only Ionos offers equivalent storage on its entry-level plans. Shared and WordPress hosting keep costs low by splitting a single server’s resources (like storage and processing power) between numerous websites. This is great for starter sites, and InMotion Hosting’s storage is atypically enormous, but limitations can still make shared and WordPress hosting unsuitable for complex or high-traffic sites. VPS, dedicated and cloud hosting InMotion offers VPS and dedicated hosting for high-traffic websites and unique builds requiring server customization. Its VPS hosting is relatively cheap, but it’s entirely unmanaged , so you’ll need to either maintain the server yourself or pay someone else to do it. InMotion Hosting’s dedicated hosting, meanwhile, is extremely expensive, so I recommend Ionos for a more affordable solution. InMotion’s cloud hosting targets enterprise businesses, with prices to match. Hostinger offers more affordable cloud hosting. Ease of use: Underwhelming, especially for first-time website owners Key takeaway: InMotion’s purchase process, account management and website management tools aren’t as user-friendly as those offered by top web hosts like SiteGround and Hostinger. I signed up for a WordPress hosting plan and built a website to test InMotion’s usability, focusing on how beginners might experience it. I repeatedly got frustrated with the awkward, overly complicated interface and tools. Power users like developers or website administrators might find these systems worthwhile, as InMotion makes it easy to access cPanel for complex tasks, but first-time website owners who don’t want to learn cPanel (and anyone seeking a simple website creation experience) should look elsewhere. The purchase process includes sneaky upsells InMotion Hosting’s checkout page has more upsells that you’ll need to pay attention to. Screenshot by Dianna Gunn/CNET InMotion’s pricing is relatively transparent, and the purchase process is straightforward, but it includes some unfortunate upsells. Plan pages clearly list both introductory and renewal prices, something that isn’t always true of other web hosts. However, it’s unclear until checkout that you’ll need to sign up – and pay for – a year or more upfront to get the lowest possible pricing, which can lead to sticker shock. Selecting a plan sends you to a domain registration page, followed by a checkout page. This seems straightforward, but you’ll need to pay close attention as InMotion automatically opts you into a backup add-on and a free trial for email hosting. Email hosting and backups are great, but you may want to opt out of these add-ons for savings or to use other systems. Alternatively, you can choose SiteGround or Ionos to get backups and email bundled into your web hosting package. Account management is overwhelming Managing your account with InMotion Hosting isn’t as user-friendly as with other web hosts. Screenshot by Dianna Gunn/CNET InMotion’s account dashboard clearly displays everything you need, including billing and account management, which other hosts often hide in secondary menus. Unfortunately, it also displays many things you’re unlikely to need, creating an overwhelming (and hideous) experience. I much prefer the streamlined account dashboards of SiteGround and Hostinger. Website and server management tools aren’t great, especially for beginners Newcomers may find InMotion Hosting’s website and server management tools cumbersome. InMotion’s website and server management tools are functional, but they’re not very user-friendly. The WordPress installer is hideous and lacks guidance. Server management is entirely done through cPanel, a tool aimed at developers, whereas other hosts offer simplified systems for basic tasks like altering DNS records. I recommend choosing an alternative like SiteGround or Hostinger if you’re looking for a simple website creation experience, as they provide more WordPress guidance and intuitive server management tools. There are three WordPress setup options: quick installation and custom installation for new websites, and quick migration for existing sites. Quick installation only installs WordPress with the default theme, an anti-spam plug-in and a form-building plug-in. Custom installation provides options for preinstalling form-building and social media sharing plug-ins, but doesn’t offer nearly the same level of guidance as setup wizards from companies like SiteGround. WordPress setup offers multiple options. Screenshot by Dianna Gunn/CNET InMotion’s WordPress installs are basic, directing you to the regular dashboard rather than a hub like those offered by SiteGround and Ionos. This is fine for experienced users and folks interested in learning new tech, but it may overwhelm first-time WordPress users seeking a simple website-creation experience. There’s a separate area for WordPress management, with some interesting options like enabling auto-updates and setting up blockers to prevent AI scrapers or other harmful bots from accessing your site. These tools are great, but like InMotion’s account dashboard, the WordPress management area is hideous and clunky, creating an especially poor experience for beginners. InMotion Hosting uses the industry-standard cPanel for server management. Screenshot by Dianna Gunn/CNET Server management, including DNS editing — something most web hosts offer simplified proprietary tools for — is done through cPanel. As the industry standard for many years, cPanel will be familiar to most technical users, such as developers, but it’s not intuitive for first-time website owners. While there is some value in learning cPanel in case you switch to another host later on, I strongly prefer the simplified server management tools provided by SiteGround and Hostinger. Performance: Thoroughly disappointing Key takeaway: My InMotion site had significant downtime and unpleasantly long loading times. This suggests that visitors won’t be able to quickly or reliably access your website if you use InMotion. I spent one week tracking uptime and site speed to determine how reliably and quickly visitors can access InMotion websites. Uptime is the percentage of time your site spends online and available to visitors. The best web hosts guarantee at least 99.9% uptime, so server issues shouldn’t cause more than 10 minutes of downtime per week. Site speed is the number of seconds your site takes to load. Experts recommend aiming for two seconds or less, as conversion rates decrease by 1% to 3% for every additional 100ms after the 2-second mark. InMotion disappointed me on both of these fronts, with the highest downtime of any host I’ve tested in 2026 and site speed well above the recommended 2-second maximum. I recommend choosing a different host, such as Hostinger or SiteGround, to ensure fast, reliable performance. Uptime was poor InMotion’s WordPress hosting plans guarantee 99.99% uptime, meaning server issues shouldn’t cause more than two minutes of downtime per week. I monitored my site with BetterStack for one week and was disappointed to find that InMotion doesn’t live up to this guarantee. In fact, my site had over 20 minutes of downtime, showing that InMotion doesn’t even live up to the industry-standard 99.9% uptime guarantee. Admittedly, this is much better than my 2024 InMotion Hosting tests — when I experienced over an hour of downtime — but it’s still not great. SiteGround, Hostinger and Ionos all had significantly less downtime during my tests. Speed is disappointing I used WebPageTest to simulate loading my site from various locations at different times of day, resulting in the following averages (measured in seconds): Location US UK Germany India Dubai Australia Global Desktop 1.6 2.09 2.27 3.71 4.45 4.62 3.12 Mobile 3.26 3.59 3.82 5.77 5.34 6.42 4.17 Combined, these numbers average 3.64 seconds, well over the recommended 2-second maximum. This is also the second-worst site speed I’ve encountered so far in my 2026 web hosting tests. Additionally, there was a major discrepancy between US and European loading times — which stayed near, or even below, the 2-second mark — and loading times in India, Dubai and Australia. You may have better results in these locations if your site is stored in a server closer to them, but if your audience is truly global, you’re better off choosing a different company like Hostinger. You can improve site speed on your own by taking actions such as installing a CDN or content delivery network to reduce loading times for international users. However, I recommend choosing a host with more reliable servers instead, such as Hostinger. Performance tools are lacking InMotion’s basic shared hosting plan doesn’t include any performance tools. Higher-level shared hosting and WordPress hosting plans feature server-side caching, which stores static data (information that isn’t updated regularly) in a fast-access layer to improve site speed. Caching is automatically enabled on these plans, so you don’t need to adjust any settings to access its benefits. Unfortunately, InMotion doesn’t offer a CDN on any plans. CDNs can improve site speed for international users by storing data in an interconnected network of global servers, letting their devices retrieve information from a server close to their location. InMotion Hosting users will need to manually connect a third-party CDN to your website to gain these benefits. Security: Solid protection from various threats, but little recourse if something goes wrong Key takeaway: InMotion includes most of the security tools and protocols I look for in a web host, but the lack of built-in automated backups is disappointing. Every InMotion plan includes the following features to encrypt your data, block malware and prevent attacks: SSL certification : A protocol for encrypting data sent to and from your site, like email addresses submitted through your contact form. Browsers, VPNs and Google use SSL to verify site safety, making sites without it harder to find and access. Firewall : Software that filters, identifies, and blocks malware and suspicious traffic. Firewalls may not protect against 100% of threats, but a regularly updated firewall can block most common threats. DDoS protection: Protocols and software for blocking distributed denial-of-service, or DDoS, attacks, which send floods of malicious traffic to your site with the intent of overwhelming your server and shutting your site down. Malware scanning: A tool for finding viruses and other malware that get past the firewall (run through cPanel). These are the core security measures you need to safely run a website, and what I’ve come to expect from most top web hosts. However, InMotion lacks automated backups — which are essential for quickly restoring your site if problems occur — unless you buy an add-on. The add-on is relatively inexpensive ($35 a year), but still notable when compared to companies like SiteGround and Ionos, which include daily automated backups in all plans. Customer service: Some of it is great, some of it isn’t Key takeaway: InMotion’s customer support is highly variable, with a mediocre knowledge base, excellent online support and poor phone support. I analyzed InMotion’s knowledge base and contacted the company via live chat, email and phone to test its troubleshooting capabilities. I enjoyed rapid, helpful responses via live chat and email, but struggled to reach a representative by phone. The support center also wasn’t great, with few images and no videos. I recommend choosing SiteGround or Ionos for better, more consistent support. Knowledge base and tutorials lack visual materials The knowledge base has fewer visuals than I’d like. Screenshot by Dianna Gunn/CNET InMotion’s support center has a clean, modern layout and quick links to questions about various hosting types and other common query categories. Individual articles use beginner-friendly language and step-by-step instructions. However, most of the tutorials I explored lacked images, and none included videos, which may disappoint visual learners. Companies like SiteGround and Ionos have better image-to-text ratios in their support articles, while Hostinger offers numerous video guides. Direct communication is inconsistent I contacted InMotion via live chat, email and phone. Live chat — both with the AI-powered bot and with human support — was fast and helpful, as was email support. However, phone support took ages to access, and I had to wait for multiple teams to confirm the information I needed. I recommend looking elsewhere if you prefer phone support. My first point of contact was an AI chatbot, which automatically searched for team members when I opened the chat. After a minute of searching, the bot informed me that wait times were higher than usual and offered to help me itself. I accepted the offer and found it very helpful, providing detailed answers to my questions and links to tutorials for further information. I asked to speak to a human, and the bot redirected me to human support without further questions, but it warned me that response times were “longer than usual” and it might take 15 minutes to connect to someone. The wait was about 10 minutes, 5 minutes faster than expected. The agent was polite and helpful, successfully answering my questions and wrapping up the conversation within a few minutes. I then submitted a ticket for email support and was pleasantly surprised to receive a response in 15 minutes — on par with the response time from SiteGround, generally considered the industry leader in customer service. The response was polite and helpful, resolving my problem without needing further follow-ups. Finally, I called InMotion’s technical support team. I received an automated warning that wait times were over half an hour and was encouraged to switch to live chat for faster customer service. I stayed on the line and waited for 40 minutes before speaking with an agent. The representative was polite and helpful, but had to confirm things with a more advanced support team, resulting in another 10 minutes spent on hold. I spent roughly an hour on the phone in total, and while they resolved my queries, I was frustrated by the entire experience. Reputation is mostly good, with some concerns InMotion has a 4.6 out of 5 star rating on Trustpilot, with most of the positive reviews citing excellent customer support. However, InMotion also has over 450 one-star reviews — a full 16% of the roughly 3,000 total reviews — and most of them say the quality of customer service has declined in recent months. This suggests InMotion’s customer support may be inconsistent, and whether you receive a timely solution depends on when you make your request and which agent you speak to. InMotion can work for tech-savvy users, but it’s not the best choice InMotion’s tools are effective, but they’re not beginner-friendly. Instead, it seems aimed at power users, with an old-school interface and easy access to cPanel for advanced server management. However, even seasoned users may want to look elsewhere, as my site had high downtime and poor site speed. InMotion’s introductory costs are also unusually high, so you won’t even save money by using it. I recommend beginners look to Hostinger or SiteGround instead, while advanced users like developers will be better served by Ionos or Hosting.com.
